otago-gold-rush.name: Otago Gold Rush
otago-gold-rush.summary: New Zealand's biggest gold strike, occurring in Central Otago during the 1860s and drawing up to 18,000 miners, many veterans of the California and Victoria rushes.

dunedin.name: Dunedin
dunedin.summary: Second-most populous city in New Zealand's South Island, named after the Scottish Gaelic name for Edinburgh, with roots in a 19th-century gold rush.

joseph-dalton-hooker.name: Joseph Dalton Hooker
joseph-dalton-hooker.summary: English botanist and explorer, a founder of geographical botany and Charles Darwin's closest friend, who directed Kew's Royal Botanic Gardens for 20 years.

joseph-maiden.name: Joseph Maiden
joseph-maiden.summary: Botanist who made major contributions to knowledge of Australian flora, especially the genus Eucalyptus.

guangdong.name: Guangdong
guangdong.summary: A coastal province in South China, home to Guangzhou and Shenzhen, historically the starting point of the ancient Maritime Silk Road.

cantonese-cuisine.name: Cantonese cuisine
cantonese-cuisine.summary: The cuisine of Cantonese-speaking people from China's Guangdong province, one of China's Eight Great Traditions and, through emigration, the style behind most Chinese restaurants in the West until the late 20th century.

bay-of-plenty.name: Bay of Plenty
bay-of-plenty.summary: A large bay on New Zealand's North Island, named by James Cook in 1769 after seeing the abundant food at nearby Māori villages.

sweet-potato.name: Kūmara
sweet-potato.summary: A starchy, sweet-tasting root vegetable native to tropical South America, a staple food in many regions and only distantly related to the true potato.

tapu-polynesian-culture.name: Tapu
tapu-polynesian-culture.summary: A Polynesian concept of something holy or sacred involving rules and prohibitions; the source of the English word "taboo", from Captain Cook's 1777 visit to Tonga.

billardiera-scandens.name: Billardiera scandens
billardiera-scandens.summary: A small Australian shrub or twining plant, also called hairy apple berry, that produces oblong berries covered in fine hair and was once described as almost the country's only wild edible fruit.

rarotonga.name: Rarotonga
rarotonga.summary: Largest and most populous island of the Cook Islands, home to about 72% of the country's population and its capital, Avarua.

ferdinand-bauer.name: Ferdinand Bauer
ferdinand-bauer.summary: Austrian botanical illustrator (1760–1826) who traveled on Matthew Flinders' expedition to Australia.

matthew-flinders.name: Matthew Flinders
matthew-flinders.summary: British navigator (1774–1814) who led the first inshore circumnavigation of Australia and is credited with popularising the continent's name.

charles-alexandre-lesueur.name: Charles-Alexandre Lesueur
charles-alexandre-lesueur.summary: French naturalist, artist and explorer (1778-1846) who collected specimens in Australia, Southeast Asia and North America and described several new species.

nicolas-baudin.name: Nicolas Baudin
nicolas-baudin.summary: French explorer, cartographer and naturalist (1754–1803) best known for his expeditions to Australia and the southern Pacific Ocean.

victorian-gold-rush.name: Victorian gold rush
victorian-gold-rush.summary: A gold rush in the Australian colony of Victoria lasting roughly from 1851 to the late 1860s, bringing great prosperity and rapid population growth to Melbourne.

ballarat.name: Ballarat
ballarat.summary: A city in Victoria, Australia, whose 1851 gold discovery sparked the Victorian gold rush; site of the 1854 Eureka Rebellion, seen as the origin of Australian democracy.

bendigo.name: Bendigo
bendigo.summary: An Australian city in Victoria, formerly named Sandhurst, that grew into one of colonial Australia's largest gold-mining boomtowns after gold was found there in 1851.

italianate-architecture.name: Italianate architecture
italianate-architecture.summary: A 19th-century architectural style inspired by 16th-century Italian Renaissance buildings, first developed in Britain around 1802 and later hugely popular in the United States.

victorian-architecture.name: Victorian architecture
victorian-architecture.summary: A group of revival building styles from the mid-to-late 19th century, named after Britain's Queen Victoria and often reinterpreting older historic styles.

art-gallery-of-new-south-wales.name: Art Gallery of New South Wales
art-gallery-of-new-south-wales.summary: Sydney's most important public art gallery, founded in 1872 as the New South Wales Academy of Art and renamed the Art Gallery of New South Wales in 1880.
art-gallery-of-new-south-wales.source_title: Art Gallery of New South Wales

eliezer-levi-montefiore.name: Eliezer Levi Montefiore
eliezer-levi-montefiore.summary: A businessman and art enthusiast born in Barbados in 1820, who became the first director of the Art Gallery of New South Wales.

conrad-martens.name: Conrad Martens
conrad-martens.summary: English-born landscape painter (1801–1878) who sailed on HMS Beagle before settling in Australia, where he painted until his death.

s-t-gill.name: S. T. Gill
s-t-gill.summary: An English-born Australian artist who lived from 1818 to 1880.

william-barak.name: William Barak
william-barak.summary: Last traditional elder (ngurungaeta) of the Wurundjeri-willam clan of Melbourne (c. 1823–1903), an influential Aboriginal rights advocate and artist who recorded traditional ceremonies.

wurundjeri.name: Wurundjeri
wurundjeri.summary: Aboriginal Australian people of the Woiwurrung language group and traditional owners of the Yarra River Valley, including the area that is now Melbourne, still living there today.

ian-potter-centre-ngv-australia.name: Ian Potter Centre
ian-potter-centre-ngv-australia.summary: An art gallery at Federation Square in Melbourne housing the Australian collection of the National Gallery of Victoria.

national-gallery-of-victoria.name: National Gallery of Victoria
national-gallery-of-victoria.summary: Australia's oldest and most visited art museum, founded in Melbourne in 1861, with over 76,000 works across two sites.

art-gallery-of-ballarat.name: Art Gallery of Ballarat
art-gallery-of-ballarat.summary: Australia's oldest regional art gallery, established in 1884 in Ballarat, with a collection of more than 11,200 works from the 18th century to today.

john-lewin.name: John Lewin
john-lewin.summary: English-born artist and the first professional artist in colonial New South Wales, known for illustrating early Australian natural history, especially native birds on native plants.

john-gould.name: John Gould
john-gould.summary: English ornithologist known for The Birds of Australia; his identification of what became known as Darwin's finches helped inspire Darwin's theory of evolution by natural selection.

gothic-revival-architecture.name: Gothic Revival architecture
gothic-revival-architecture.summary: An architectural movement reviving medieval Gothic styles, becoming widespread in the first half of the 19th century and dominant in the West until the 1880s.

charles-darwin.name: Charles Darwin
charles-darwin.summary: English naturalist and biologist (1809-1882) known for his theory of evolution by natural selection, described as one of history's most influential figures.

augustus-earle.name: Augustus Earle
augustus-earle.summary: English painter (1793–1838) who travelled widely and independently, documenting European contact and colonisation in the early 19th century.

hms-beagle.name: HMS Beagle
hms-beagle.summary: A Royal Navy survey ship launched in 1820, famous for its second voyage carrying naturalist Charles Darwin, whose observations informed his theory of evolution.

ford-madox-brown.name: Ford Madox Brown
ford-madox-brown.summary: British painter (1821–1893) of moral and historical subjects in a Pre-Raphaelite style, best known for his painting Work and the twelve Manchester Murals depicting the city's history.

arthur-streeton.name: Arthur Streeton
arthur-streeton.summary: An Australian landscape painter (1867–1943) and leading member of the Heidelberg School, also known as Australian Impressionism.

tom-roberts.name: Tom Roberts
tom-roberts.summary: English-born Australian artist (1856-1931) and leading figure of the Heidelberg School (Australian impressionism), known for national narrative paintings such as Shearing the Rams.

frederick-mccubbin.name: Frederick McCubbin
frederick-mccubbin.summary: Australian painter and teacher, a leading figure of the Heidelberg School of Australian impressionism, known for large landscapes on settlers' lives in the bush, including On the Wallaby Track (1896).

eureka-rebellion.name: Eureka Rebellion
eureka-rebellion.summary: An 1851–1854 revolt by gold miners against British colonial administration in Victoria, Australia, culminating in the Battle of the Eureka Stockade on 3 December 1854, which left at least 27 dead.

liverpool-plains.name: Liverpool Plains
liverpool-plains.summary: An agricultural area of about 12,000 km2 in north-western New South Wales, Australia, drained by the Namoi River and its tributaries.

black-war.name: Black War
black-war.summary: A period of violent conflict from the mid-1820s to 1832 between British colonists and Aboriginal Tasmanians, which led to the near-extermination of the Indigenous population.

george-augustus-robinson.name: George Augustus Robinson
george-augustus-robinson.summary: English-born builder turned self-trained preacher (1791–1866), employed by British colonial authorities to 'conciliate' Indigenous Tasmanians during the Black War and later oversee their exile to Flinders Island.

flinders-island.name: Flinders Island
flinders-island.summary: A 1,367-square-kilometre island off Tasmania in the Bass Strait, part of the Furneaux Group, in the latitude zone known as the Roaring Forties.

waterloo-creek-massacre.name: Waterloo Creek massacre
waterloo-creek-massacre.summary: A series of violent clashes between mounted settlers and Indigenous Gamilaraay people near Moree, Australia, in 1837–1838, now recognized as a significant site of frontier violence.

myall-creek-massacre.name: Myall Creek massacre
myall-creek-massacre.summary: The killing of at least 28 unarmed Aboriginal people by eight colonists in New South Wales on 10 June 1838; seven perpetrators were convicted of murder and hanged.

fort-dundas.name: Fort Dundas
fort-dundas.summary: A short-lived British settlement on Melville Island, Australia, from 1824 to 1828, the first of four early attempts to settle northern Australia before Darwin was founded.

melville-island-northern-territory.name: Melville Island
melville-island-northern-territory.summary: An island off Australia's Northern Territory, part of the Tiwi Islands and roughly the size of Canada's Prince Edward Island.

tiwi-people.name: Tiwi people
tiwi-people.summary: An Aboriginal Australian people of nearly 2,000 living on the Tiwi Islands, speaking a language isolate; their society is matrilineal and blends Dreamtime beliefs with Roman Catholicism.

bendigo-petition.name: Bendigo Petition
bendigo-petition.summary: An 1853 petition by miners in colonial Victoria demanding lower gold-license fees and better land access from Governor La Trobe; most demands were rejected.

charles-la-trobe.name: Charles La Trobe
charles-la-trobe.summary: British colonial official (1801–1875) who served as superintendent of the Port Phillip District and then first lieutenant-governor of the colony of Victoria, supporting institutions like Melbourne's Botanic Gardens and university.

james-scobie.name: James Scobie
james-scobie.summary: Scottish gold digger murdered at Ballarat, Australia in 1854; the unresolved case over his death helped spark the Eureka Rebellion.

darling-downs.name: Darling Downs
darling-downs.summary: A farming region on Queensland's Great Dividing Range in Australia, named in 1827 by explorer Allan Cunningham, known for fertile clay soils and diverse agriculture.

wide-bay-burnett.name: Wide Bay
wide-bay-burnett.summary: A coastal region of Queensland, Australia, north of Brisbane, named by explorer James Cook and later a site of settler conflict and port trade.

maryborough-queensland.name: Maryborough
maryborough-queensland.summary: A city in the Fraser Coast Region of Queensland, Australia, with a population of about 15,287 in the 2021 census.

kilcoy-queensland.name: Kilcoy, Queensland
kilcoy-queensland.summary: A rural town in the Somerset Region of Queensland, Australia, with a population of about 2,000.

multuggerah.name: Multuggerah
multuggerah.summary: Aboriginal Australian leader (c. 1810–1846) of the Ugarapul nation who united Aboriginal clans in armed resistance against British troops and settlers in Queensland's Lockyer Valley in the 1840s.

battle-of-one-tree-hill.name: Battle of One Tree Hill
battle-of-one-tree-hill.summary: An 1840s battle in the Darling Downs, Australia, in which Aboriginal warrior Multuggerah and his Ugarapul fighters routed a group of European settlers, a rare pitched battle won by Indigenous forces.

anna-maria-bunn.name: Anna Maria Bunn
anna-maria-bunn.summary: Anonymous author, later identified, of The Guardian: a Tale (1838), the first novel published on mainland Australia and the first there by a woman.

ethel-turner.name: Ethel Turner
ethel-turner.summary: English-born Australian novelist and children's literature writer (1870–1958).

seven-little-australians.name: Seven Little Australians
seven-little-australians.summary: An 1894 Australian children's novel by Ethel Turner about seven mischievous siblings and their stepmother in 1880s Sydney, continuously in print for over a century.

william-wentworth.name: William Wentworth
william-wentworth.summary: Australian statesman, explorer and newspaper editor (1790–1872) who advocated self-government and press freedom, helped found the University of Sydney, and in 1813 helped lead the first crossing of the Blue Mountains.

australasia-poem.name: Australasia
australasia-poem.summary: A poem by William Charles Wentworth, published in 1823 as the first book of verse written by a native-born Australian poet.

henry-handel-richardson.name: Henry Handel Richardson
henry-handel-richardson.summary: Pen name of Ethel Florence Lindesay Richardson (1870 to 1946), an Australian author.

the-getting-of-wisdom.name: The Getting of Wisdom
the-getting-of-wisdom.summary: 1910 novel by Australian novelist Henry Handel Richardson, almost continuously in print ever since.

h-g-wells.name: H. G. Wells
h-g-wells.summary: English writer (1866–1946) of more than forty novels, often called the 'father of science fiction' for works like The Time Machine that imagined time travel and alien invasion.

germaine-greer.name: Germaine Greer
germaine-greer.summary: Australian writer and public intellectual (born 1939), a major voice of second-wave feminism whose 1970 book The Female Eunuch became an international bestseller.

charles-harpur.name: Charles Harpur
charles-harpur.summary: Australian poet and playwright (1813–1868) regarded as Australia's most important 19th-century poet.

henry-kendall-poet.name: Henry Kendall
henry-kendall-poet.summary: Australian author and bush poet (1839–1882), known for poems and tales set in the natural environment.

james-unaipon.name: James Unaipon
james-unaipon.summary: Australian Indigenous preacher (c. 1835–1907) of the Ngarrindjeri people, the first Aboriginal deacon and father of inventor David Unaipon.

ngarrindjeri.name: Ngarrindjeri
ngarrindjeri.summary: The traditional Aboriginal people of the lower Murray River, eastern Fleurieu Peninsula and the Coorong in South Australia, formed from several distinct tribal groups united under one cultural identity.

george-taplin.name: George Taplin
george-taplin.summary: Congregationalist minister who worked in Aboriginal missions in South Australia and wrote about Ngarrindjeri lore and customs, gaining a reputation as an anthropologist.

david-unaipon.name: David Unaipon
david-unaipon.summary: An Aboriginal Australian author, inventor and preacher (1872–1967) who wrote essays and stories drawn from oral traditions, held ten patents, and by the late 1920s was one of Australia's best-known Aboriginal people.

sydney-observatory.name: Sydney Observatory
sydney-observatory.summary: A heritage-listed astronomical observatory and museum on Observatory Hill in Sydney, built between 1857 and 1859 on the site of a former fort.

observatory-park-sydney.name: Observatory Hill
observatory-park-sydney.summary: A park in central Sydney, Australia, site of the colony's first windmill and later the historic Sydney Observatory, plus the remains of a fort and signal station.

william-farrer.name: William Farrer
william-farrer.summary: English-born Australian agronomist and plant breeder (1845–1906), known as the 'father of the Australian wheat industry' for developing the 'Federation' wheat variety, released in 1903.

great-melbourne-telescope.name: Great Melbourne Telescope
great-melbourne-telescope.summary: Built in Dublin in 1868 and installed at Melbourne Observatory in 1869, it had a 48-inch mirror, one of the largest telescopes of its era, later moved and damaged by bushfire.

grubb-parsons.name: Grubb Telescope Company
grubb-parsons.summary: An Irish telescope manufacturer founded in Dublin in 1833 by Thomas Grubb, which built some of the largest research telescopes of the 19th century before later becoming Grubb Parsons.

melbourne-observatory.name: Melbourne Observatory
melbourne-observatory.summary: An astronomical observatory in Melbourne, Australia, operating since 1863, which housed the Great Melbourne Telescope from 1869.

lawrence-hargrave.name: Lawrence Hargrave
lawrence-hargrave.summary: Australian engineer and aeronautical pioneer, 1850 to 1915, best known for inventing the box kite, which later formed the aerodynamic basis of early biplanes.

ernest-rutherford.name: Ernest Rutherford
ernest-rutherford.summary: New Zealand physicist and chemist (1871–1937), called the father of nuclear physics, who won the 1908 Nobel Prize in Chemistry and later proposed the atomic nucleus.

university-of-canterbury.name: Canterbury College
university-of-canterbury.summary: The original name, from its 1873 founding, of what became the University of Canterbury in Christchurch, New Zealand, then a constituent college of the University of New Zealand.

university-of-new-zealand.name: University of New Zealand
university-of-new-zealand.summary: New Zealand's sole degree-granting university from 1874 to 1961, a collegiate institution whose colleges later became independent universities including Canterbury and Auckland.

cavendish-laboratory.name: Cavendish Laboratory
cavendish-laboratory.summary: The physics department of the University of Cambridge, opened in 1874, where researchers discovered the electron, the neutron, and the structure of DNA.

william-scott-astronomer-and-priest.name: William Scott
william-scott-astronomer-and-priest.summary: William Scott: Church of England priest (1825–1917) who became the colonial astronomer for New South Wales.

red-fife-wheat.name: Red Fife wheat
red-fife-wheat.summary: A hardy Canadian bread wheat first grown in 1842 from Ukrainian seed, dominant in Canadian and northern US wheat farming from the mid-1800s to the early 1900s, also known as Canadian Fife.

stanwell-park.name: Stanwell Park
stanwell-park.summary: A coastal village and northern suburb of Wollongong, New South Wales, Australia, in a small valley south of Sydney's Royal National Park.

carte-du-ciel.name: Astrographic Catalogue
carte-du-ciel.summary: Part of a late-19th-century international project to map millions of stars, in which twenty observatories exposed and measured over 22,000 photographic plates over several decades.

south-australia-act-1834.name: South Australia Act 1834
south-australia-act-1834.summary: An 1834 act of the UK Parliament authorizing the founding of the colony of South Australia, setting its boundaries and creating a London-based commission to oversee land sales.

john-verran.name: John Verran
john-verran.summary: Australian politician and trade unionist (1856–1932) who served as premier of South Australia from 1910 to 1912, the second Labor premier there.

australian-constitutions-act-1850.name: Australian Colonies Government Act 1850
australian-constitutions-act-1850.summary: An 1850 act of the UK Parliament that created the Colony of Victoria and set up new constitutions, with bicameral parliaments, for New South Wales, Victoria, South Australia and Tasmania.

constitution-of-australia.name: Australian Constitution Act
constitution-of-australia.summary: The 1900 act of the UK Parliament that enacted Australia's founding constitution, taking effect on 1 January 1901 and uniting six British colonies into a federal Commonwealth.

william-hobson.name: William Hobson
william-hobson.summary: Royal Navy officer and first governor of New Zealand (1792–1842), co-author of the 1840 Treaty of Waitangi who proclaimed British sovereignty over New Zealand and chose the site of Auckland.

treaty-of-waitangi.name: Treaty of Waitangi
treaty-of-waitangi.summary: Document first signed on 6 February 1840 by a British consul and Māori chiefs, central to New Zealand's national identity and to disputes over whether Māori ceded sovereignty to the Crown.

new-zealand-wars.name: New Zealand Wars
new-zealand-wars.summary: Conflicts from 1845 to 1872 between the New Zealand colonial government and allied Māori against other Māori and settlers, which escalated over disputed land sales and Crown sovereignty.

south-australia-act-1842.name: South Australia Act 1842
south-australia-act-1842.summary: An 1842 UK act that repealed the 1834 South Australia Act and gave Britain full control of the colony as a Crown Colony after it neared bankruptcy in 1840.

lachlan-macquarie.name: Lachlan Macquarie
lachlan-macquarie.summary: British Army officer who served as the fifth Governor of New South Wales from 1810 to 1821, shaping Sydney's layout and Australia's shift from penal colony to free settlement.

emancipist.name: Emancipist
emancipist.summary: A term for a convict transported to Australia who was freed by the governor, gaining rights such as landownership though often still shunned socially by free settlers.

george-reid.name: George Reid
george-reid.summary: Fourth prime minister of Australia (1904–1905) and Free Trade Party leader, who earlier served as premier of New South Wales from 1894 to 1899.

liberal-party-australia-1909.name: Commonwealth Liberal Party
liberal-party-australia-1909.summary: Australian political party (1909–1917) formed by merging the Protectionist and Anti-Socialist parties, creating the country's first two-party system under Alfred Deakin.

new-holland-australia.name: New Holland
new-holland-australia.summary: A historical European name for mainland Australia, applied by the Dutch from 1644 and used semi-officially until the mid-1850s before being replaced by 'Australia'.

john-plunkett.name: John Plunkett
john-plunkett.summary: John Plunkett: Attorney-General of New South Wales (1802–1869), also an appointed member of the colony's Legislative Council for decades.

church-act-1836.name: Church Act 1836
church-act-1836.summary: An 1836 New South Wales law that funded Church of England, Church of Scotland and Catholic churches equally, ending the Church of England's privileged status there.

gregory-blaxland.name: Gregory Blaxland
gregory-blaxland.summary: An English-born pioneer farmer and explorer who lived from 1778 to 1853.

william-lawson-explorer.name: William Lawson
william-lawson-explorer.summary: British soldier, explorer and politician (1774–1850) who in 1813 helped pioneer the first crossing of Australia's Blue Mountains, opening inland pastures that fueled the colony's growth.

blue-mountains-new-south-wales.name: Blue Mountains
blue-mountains-new-south-wales.summary: A mountainous region on the western edge of Sydney, Australia, forming part of the Great Dividing Range.

andrew-fisher.name: Andrew Fisher
andrew-fisher.summary: The fifth prime minister of Australia (1908–1909, 1910–1913, 1914–1915) and Labor Party leader who led it to its first federal election victory in 1910.

commonwealth-bank.name: Commonwealth Bank
commonwealth-bank.summary: An Australian multinational bank founded by the government in 1911 and fully privatised in 1996, now one of Australia's 'big four' banks.

w-r-boyce-gibson.name: W. R. Boyce Gibson
w-r-boyce-gibson.summary: British-Australian philosopher (1869–1935) who advocated personal idealism.

william-mitchell-philosopher.name: Sir William Mitchell
william-mitchell-philosopher.summary: Scottish-born Australian philosopher and academic (1861–1962), professor at the University of Adelaide from 1894 and later its vice-chancellor and chancellor.

section-116-of-the-constitution-of-austr.name: Section 116
section-116-of-the-constitution-of-austr.summary: A clause in Australia's constitution barring the federal government from establishing a religion or requiring religious tests for public office, interpreted narrowly by courts ever since.
section-116-of-the-constitution-of-austr.source_title: Section 116 of the Constitution of Australia

castle-hill-convict-rebellion.name: Castle Hill Rebellion
castle-hill-convict-rebellion.summary: An 1804 convict uprising near Sydney led by veterans of the 1798 Irish Rebellion, suppressed under Australia's first declaration of martial law.

marree-mosque.name: Marree Mosque
marree-mosque.summary: A former mosque located in Marree, South Australia.

central-adelaide-mosque.name: Central Adelaide Mosque
central-adelaide-mosque.summary: The oldest permanent mosque in Australia, built in 1888–1889 in Adelaide to serve Afghan cameleers and traders, with its four minarets added in 1903.

raukkan-south-australia.name: Point McLeay Mission
raukkan-south-australia.summary: A Christian mission established in 1859 for the Ngarrindjeri people, later made an Aboriginal reserve in 1916 and handed back to the Ngarrindjeri in 1974, renamed Raukkan in 1982.

the-ashes.name: The Ashes
the-ashes.summary: A term from an 1882 satirical obituary declaring English cricket "dead" with its "ashes taken to Australia," which came to name the England–Australia Test cricket series.

theatre-royal-hobart.name: Theatre Royal, Hobart
theatre-royal-hobart.summary: A historic theatre in Hobart, Tasmania, and the oldest continually operating theatre in Australia; Noël Coward called it "a dream of a theatre".

queen-s-theatre-adelaide.name: Queen's Theatre, Adelaide
queen-s-theatre-adelaide.summary: The oldest intact theatre on mainland Australia, originally built in Adelaide in 1840, later reopened under other names before being restored as a performance venue in 1996.

melbourne-cricket-ground.name: Melbourne Cricket Ground
melbourne-cricket-ground.summary: A major stadium in Melbourne, Australia, established in 1853, where the first Test cricket match was played in 1877.

test-cricket.name: Test match
test-cricket.summary: The oldest and most prestigious format of international cricket, played over up to five days between national teams; the term was coined in 1861-62 and became official in the 1890s.

sheffield-shield.name: Sheffield Shield
sheffield-shield.summary: Australia's domestic first-class cricket competition, contested by teams representing the six states since it began in the 1892–93 season.

princess-theatre-melbourne.name: Princess Theatre
princess-theatre-melbourne.summary: A 1,452-seat theatre in Melbourne established in 1854 and rebuilt in 1886, it is the oldest surviving entertainment site on mainland Australia.

burke-and-wills-expedition.name: Burke and Wills expedition
burke-and-wills-expedition.summary: An 1860–61 attempt to cross Australia from Melbourne to the Gulf of Carpentaria, led by Robert Burke and William Wills; both leaders died on the return journey, and only one member completed the whole trip.

tom-wills.name: Tom Wills
tom-wills.summary: An Australian sportsman (1835–1880) regarded as Australia's first cricketer of significance, who captained the Victoria cricket team and co-wrote the 1859 laws underlying Australian rules football.

charles-lawrence-cricketer.name: Charles Lawrence
charles-lawrence-cricketer.summary: English cricketer (1828–1916) who settled in Australia and captain-coached the Aboriginal cricket team that toured England in 1868, the first Australian team ever to tour England.

ned-kelly.name: Ned Kelly
ned-kelly.summary: An Australian bushranger and gang leader (1854–1880), one of the last bushrangers, famous for wearing homemade bulletproof armour in his final shootout with police.

australia_new_zealand-industrial-art-011: Art Gallery of New South Wales
New South Wales Academy of Art
